title: Blossom Farm Products Co. v. Kasson Cheese Co., Inc.
lead: A supplier sought payment for a lawful cheese additive, but its knowing assistance in the buyer’s profitable mislabeling made the payment promise unenforceable on public-policy grounds.

actors.name: Blossom Farm Products Company
actors.role: Supplier suing to collect the last shipment’s open-account price

actors.name: Kasson Cheese Company
actors.role: Buyer labeling enhanced output as real mozzarella and provolone

actors.name: Julian Podell
actors.role: Blossom salesman and the manufacturer’s sole American distributor

actors.name: Marvin Silverman
actors.role: Manufacturer who advised on production and warned of labeling consequences

proceedings: Trial court refused to enforce the payment promise; Blossom appealed and Kasson cross-appealed; Court of Appeals affirmed dismissal and held the cross-appeal moot.
limits: The additive itself had lawful uses. The court rested on public-policy nonenforcement, not a declaration that every supply contract or sale was illegal. No criminal penalty or restitution award was imposed.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: A useful powder became part of a mislabeled cheese business
sections.cue: Explain the technical distinction that makes the conduct wrongful.
paragraphs: Blossom Farm Products Company supplied Kasson Cheese Company with Isokappacase powder from August 1981 through February 1984, grossing more than $5 million. Blossom salesman Julian Podell was the manufacturer’s sole American distributor. The powder could lawfully serve as a starter medium, prevent bacteriophages, or enhance yield.

Starter use required relatively little protein. Direct addition to cheese milk as an enhancer increased output, but because the powder contained more than seventy-five percent protein or caseins, it produced an imitation or analog product requiring corresponding labels and an accurate ingredient statement. That use was lawful with proper labeling. Kasson instead sold the output as real mozzarella and provolone.

Kasson bought about one hundred times the amount needed for starter use, and its milk volume could not explain that quantity on a starter theory. Podell knew those figures. When Kasson stopped using the enhancer after a regulatory warning, the manufacturer stopped producing it.

sections.title: The final unpaid shipment led to a public-policy defense
sections.cue: Set out the knowledge evidence supporting the trial finding.
paragraphs: Blossom sued for $138,306 on an open account for its final shipment. The trial court refused enforcement because both parties knew of and benefited from the improper use. Blossom appealed, arguing that selling a lawful enhancer remained enforceable despite knowledge that Kasson mislabeled its finished product. Kasson cross-appealed, emphasizing Blossom’s participation and benefit.

The evidence showed more than remote awareness. Manufacturer Marvin Silverman recommended a pump to solve Kasson’s clotting problem, warned its president that direct addition produced something outside real-cheese standards, inferred mislabeling from the economics, and told Podell of that conclusion. A Kasson consultant testified that Podell’s figures concerned yields and costs. Kasson’s president admitted continuing real-cheese labels while treating the practice as a legal gray area, although he had not explicitly told Podell about those labels.

The appellate court found sufficient circumstantial evidence of knowledgeable involvement and deliberate facilitation to sustain the trial finding as not clearly erroneous. It reviewed enforceability as a legal issue and framed its ruling as nonenforcement on public-policy grounds rather than calling the supply contract itself illegal.

sections.title: Knowing facilitation connected the payment promise to misbranding
sections.cue: Apply the Restatement rules and the statutory policy.
paragraphs: Under Restatement § 182, a seller that substantially performs does not ordinarily forfeit payment simply because the buyer intends an improper use. But a seller acting to further that use can be barred. Specific assistance and a continuing course of dealing can establish that purpose. Section 178 required weighing enforcement against the contrary policy, considering the policy’s legislative strength, the value of nonenforcement in advancing it, the seriousness and deliberateness of misconduct, and its direct connection to the promise.

Wisconsin legislation adopted federal standards distinguishing real and imitation cheese, establishing a concrete policy of accurate food labeling. Correctly labeled analog product would have sold for approximately seventy cents per pound rather than the $1.40 obtained through real-cheese labeling. Continued high-volume shipments with knowledge of that model facilitated and profited from the misbranding. Podell’s lack of an express admission from Kasson’s president did not erase the other evidence.

Blossom had delivered its last shipment, and a properly conducted supply relationship would have been lawful. Nevertheless, the direct, deliberate connection to misleading labels justified refusing to enforce payment.

sections.title: The collection suit remained dismissed
sections.cue: Give the cross-appeal its own disposition.
paragraphs: On September 17, 1986, Chief Judge Scott, joined by Presiding Judge Brown and Judge Nettesheim, affirmed the judgment dismissing Blossom’s collection suit. There was no separate opinion. That conclusion made Kasson’s cross-appeal moot, as the final judicial note explained.

The decision imposed no criminal sanction, ordered no restitution to either side, and did not prohibit every use or sale of the powder. It denied judicial enforcement of this payment promise because of the supplier’s knowing assistance in the mislabeled-product business.
